text: Time to work both chapter examples by hand, start to finish, with no new numbers introduced — just the ones already verified in Lessons 11 and 12, traced through carefully enough that you could reproduce them yourself.

First, the exact case. Two counting qubits, Hadamards into a uniform superposition, then qubit 0 controls U to the first power and qubit 1 controls U squared, building the joint state one half times the sum of e to the 2 pi i x over 4 times x. The inverse QFT decodes that state, and because theta equals one quarter is exactly 2 bits in binary, there's zero leftover interference. The verified result: probability of measuring k equals 1 is exactly 1.000000, and every other outcome is exactly zero.

Now the realistic case, theta equals 0.3, which never terminates in binary. With 3 counting qubits and 8 possible outcomes, the verified probabilities peak at k equals 2, estimate 0.25, at 57.75 percent — more than double the next-most-likely outcome, k equals 3 at 25.93 percent. All eight probabilities sum to exactly 1, as they must.

k equals 2 is still the right answer to report, because with only 8 discrete estimates available, the nearest representable value is the best any single measurement can be — and k equals 2 is both the most likely outcome and the one closest to the true 0.3. Reporting it isn't claiming theta is exactly 0.25, it's the honest best 3-bit estimate, with real odds of a neighboring outcome instead. Pushing past 90 percent confidence takes more counting qubits, exactly per Lesson 12's formula — the only lever available, and it comes at that same exponential cost.
Chapter 4 turns to this course's other landmark quantum speedup: Grover's algorithm, starting with the unstructured search problem it was built to solve.
